summary: Updates the POP3 mailbox protocol from RFC 1939 with a way for servers to announce which optional commands and extensions they support. A client can ask and then use only what is available. It is a proposed standard and was itself updated by RFC 5034.

eli5.summary: Before you order at a restaurant you can ask what is on the menu. This lets an email client ask a mail server what extra things it can do.

questions: what is the pop3 capa command
what does pop3 expire capability mean
how do pop3 response codes work
subtitle: How a POP3 server tells a mail client which optional commands and behaviors it offers.

tldr.problem: POP3 has optional commands and server behaviors, but a client could only find out what a server supported by trying things and seeing what failed.
tldr.mechanism: A new CAPA command makes the server list its capabilities, one per line. The RFC also defines an initial set of capabilities, extended response codes in square brackets and a formal grammar.
tldr.outcome: Clients can adapt to the server instead of probing. The RFC keeps extensions rare: POP3 is meant to stay a simple download-and-delete protocol. It updates RFC 1939 and was itself updated by RFC 5034.

today: RFC 2449 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1939, and it was itself updated by RFC 5034. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why POP3 Needed a Way to Announce Features
sections.content:
The Post Office Protocol version 3 (RFC 1939) is very widely used. It has some optional commands, and some useful extensions had been published, but it had no way to advertise them. Optional features could only be found by probing, if at all. The RFC calls this inefficient and possibly worse, and notes that some clients had manual settings for server capabilities.

This RFC updates RFC 1939 with a mechanism to announce optional commands, extensions and unconditional server behavior. It adds an initial set of capabilities, extended error codes that a program can parse, and an ABNF grammar for POP3 commands and responses.

An IESG note says the extension is for servers to express policy decisions by the administrator. It is not an endorsement of POP3 extensions generally: POP3 should stay simple, and IMAP (RFC 2060) should be used for more complicated operations.
sections.eli5: Mail programs used to have to poke a server to see what it could do. This RFC lets the server just say it up front.

sections.title: Command and Response Grammar and Lengths
sections.content:
Section 3 writes the general form of POP3 commands and responses in ABNF. A command is a keyword of 3 to 4 characters followed by zero or more space-separated parameters. A response is a greeting, a single-line response, a CAPA response or a multi-line response. A response may carry an optional response code in square brackets, and the greeting may carry a timestamp that must conform to an RFC 822 msg-id.

The RFC also raises a limit. RFC 1939 allowed a command of 47 characters. Now a command may be up to 255 octets including the final CRLF, and servers that support CAPA MUST accept that length, plus the largest command length of any capability they support. The first line of a response, including the greeting, stays at 512 octets.
sections.eli5: The RFC writes down exactly what a valid message looks like, like a rulebook for sentences, and lets the sentences be a bit longer than before.

sections.title: The CAPA Command
sections.content:
CAPA takes no arguments and returns the list of capabilities the server supports. It works in both the AUTHORIZATION and TRANSACTION states. An -ERR reply means the server does not implement CAPA, and the client has to probe as before. An +OK reply is followed by one capability per line, each a name optionally followed by space-separated parameters (at most 512 octets per line), ending with a line containing only a period.

Each capability description MUST say in which states it is announced and where its commands are valid. A capability available in AUTHORIZATION state MUST be announced in both states. This lets a client send a single CAPA command unless it needs TRANSACTION-only capabilities or values that may differ after login. If authentication negotiates an integrity protection layer, the client SHOULD send CAPA again afterwards to check for down-negotiation attacks.

There is no APOP capability. Clients learn that APOP is supported from the challenge in angle brackets in the greeting banner, so an APOP capability would be a second way to announce the same thing.
sections.eli5: The client says CAPA, which means what can you do, and the server answers with a list ending in a single dot, like the end of a shopping list.

sections.title: The Initial Set of Capabilities
sections.content:
The RFC defines nine capabilities. Three cover existing optional commands: TOP (the optional TOP command), USER (the USER and PASS commands) and UIDL (the optional UIDL command). SASL says the AUTH command is available and lists the supported SASL mechanisms.

RESP-CODES says the server's response text beginning with [ is an extended response code. PIPELINING says the server accepts several commands at once without waiting for each answer; the server MUST process them in turn and the client MUST match replies to commands in order. IMPLEMENTATION carries a string identifying the server, and clients MUST NOT change behavior based on it.

LOGIN-DELAY gives the minimum number of seconds between logins, which lets clients that have a configurable check interval stay within it. Servers that advertise it SHOULD enforce it. EXPIRE gives the minimum number of days the server keeps messages, or NEVER. EXPIRE 0 means the client may not leave mail on the server. If the value differs per user, the server announces the smallest possible value before login and appends the token USER to say a more accurate value is available after login.
sections.eli5: The server can say things like you may only visit every 900 seconds, or I keep your mail for 60 days, so your mail program knows the house rules.

sections.title: Extended Response Codes
sections.content:
Plain POP3 can only say success or failure. Clients often need the reason, especially for a failed login. Some widely deployed clients tried to decode the error text of a failed PASS to tell a locked maildrop from a bad login. This RFC allows an optional response code in square brackets at the start of the human readable text of an +OK or -ERR response. A server that supports them advertises the RESP-CODES capability.

Codes are case-insensitive and hierarchical, with / separating levels of detail. Clients MUST ignore unknown detail, so more can be added later, and MAY strip bracketed text before showing the message to the user.

Two codes are defined. LOGIN-DELAY appears on an -ERR to AUTH, USER, PASS or APOP and means the user logged in recently and must wait. IN-USE appears on an -ERR to AUTH, APOP or PASS and means authentication worked but the maildrop is in use, probably by another POP3 client.
sections.eli5: Instead of just saying no, the server can add a short tag like try again later or someone else is using it, so the program knows why.

sections.title: Adding New Extensions and Codes
sections.content:
Section 7 says future POP3 extensions are in general discouraged, because POP3's usefulness lies in its simplicity. It is a download-and-delete protocol, and extensions that add mailboxes, allow uploading messages or deviate from that model are strongly discouraged and unlikely to be allowed on the standards track. Clients MUST NOT require any extension for basic functionality, except the authentication commands (APOP, AUTH and USER/PASS).

IANA is asked to keep two registries, POP3 capabilities and POP3 response codes. A new capability MUST be defined in a standards track or IESG approved experimental RFC and MUST NOT begin with the letter X. It must give the CAPA tag, arguments, added commands, affected standard commands, announced states, valid states, specification reference and a discussion. A new response code needs a permanent, readily available specification (Specification Required) stating the code, which responses and commands it applies to, and its meaning and expected client behavior.
sections.eli5: New features need an official write-up before they join the list, and the club would rather not have many new features at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A capability list can reveal information about the server's authentication mechanisms, which could be used to judge whether certain attacks will work. On the other hand, letting clients detect stronger mechanisms automatically and switch to them can improve overall security at a site.

The LOGIN-DELAY response code to a USER command saves the server the work of authenticating, but it reveals that the named user exists. Unless user names are not secret in that environment, access is restricted, or the server can verify the connection is the same user, the RFC strongly recommends servers not send it in reply to USER.
sections.eli5: Telling people what locks your door has can help a burglar, but it also helps your family pick the strongest lock. And you should not confirm who lives in the house.

data.title: Example CAPA session
data.code:
C: CAPA
S: +OK Capability list follows
S: TOP
S: USER
S: SASL CRAM-MD5 KERBEROS_V4
S: RESP-CODES
S: LOGIN-DELAY 900
S: PIPELINING
S: EXPIRE 60
S: UIDL
S: IMPLEMENTATION Shlemazle-Plotz-v302
S: .

items.title: PIPELINING
items.text: Several commands may be sent at once.

items.title: EXPIRE
items.text: Minimum days messages are kept, or NEVER.

items.title: IMPLEMENTATION
items.text: A string naming the server software.
